assignment.title: Algebra II Honors — Lesson 3: Inverse Linear Functions

questions.prompt: Review ordered pairs and function notation.

responses.label: If (−3, 7) is in a relation, the swapped ordered pair is

optionRationales.0: A slope of 0 is a horizontal line; y = x rises as x increases.
optionRationales.1: y = x rises 1 unit for each unit to the right.
optionRationales.−1: A slope of −1 falls to the right, like y = −x; y = x rises.

responses.label: For inverse graphs, y=x acts as

optionRationales.the reflection line: A function and its inverse swap x and y, which mirrors the graph across y = x.
optionRationales.a vertical asymptote: y = x is a slanted line that both graphs can cross, not a vertical line they approach.
optionRationales.the x-axis: The x-axis is y = 0; y = x is the slanted line through the origin.

questions.prompt: For f(x)=3x+2, identify its domain and range.

optionRationales.(−∞, ∞): Any real number can be tripled and increased by 2, so every x is allowed.
optionRationales.(0, ∞): Every real input works, including 0 and negatives: f(0) = 2.

optionRationales.(−∞, ∞): A line with a nonzero slope reaches every real output.
optionRationales.[2, ∞): 2 is the y-intercept, not a lowest value; the line keeps going down to the left: f(−1) = −1.
optionRationales.(0, ∞): Outputs can be 0 or negative: f(−1) = −1.

optionRationales.{(26, −3), (11, 2), (−1, 6), (20, −1)}: Each pair has its x and y swapped: (−3, 26) becomes (26, −3).
optionRationales.{(−26, 3), (−11, −2), (1, −6), (−20, 1)}: This swaps the coordinates but also changes their signs; finding an inverse never changes signs.
optionRationales.{(−3, 26), (2, 11), (6, −1), (−1, 20)}: This is the relation as given; its inverse has to change each pair.

responses.label: What was done to each ordered pair?
options: reverse the order of the pairs only

optionRationales.swap x and y: An inverse undoes the relation, so each output becomes an input: (x, y) turns into (y, x).
optionRationales.change both signs: Changing both signs reflects each point through the origin; it does not undo the relation.
optionRationales.reverse the order of the pairs only: The order of the pairs in a set does not matter; listing them backward gives the same relation.

questions.prompt: Use the inverse property. If f(6)=2, complete the statement about f⁻¹.

optionRationales.(x+7)/3: Swap x and y in y = 3x − 7, then undo the steps: add 7, then divide by 3.
optionRationales.3x+7: This changes the sign of −7 but keeps multiplying by 3; an inverse also undoes the multiplication.
optionRationales.(x−7)/3: This undoes the 3 but not the −7: subtracting 7 again repeats a step of f.
optionRationales.7−3x: This is −f(x), the negative of f, not its inverse.

responses.label: Which composition should equal x if the inverse is correct?

optionRationales.f(f⁻¹(x)): Applying f⁻¹ and then f undoes every step, so you get back x.
optionRationales.f(x)+f⁻¹(x): Adding the two outputs does not undo anything; a check feeds one function into the other.
optionRationales.f(x)−f⁻¹(x): Subtracting the two outputs does not undo anything; a check feeds one function into the other.

optionRationales.(12−x)/4: Swap x and y in y = −4x + 12, subtract 12, then divide by −4.
optionRationales.(x−12)/4: This divides by 4 instead of −4, so the sign is lost; the inverse of a falling line also falls.
optionRationales.−4x−12: This changes the sign of 12 but keeps multiplying by −4; an inverse also undoes the multiplication.
optionRationales.4x+12: This changes the sign of −4 but keeps multiplying; an inverse divides instead.

optionRationales.4: This changes the sign of the slope of f instead of undoing it; the inverse undoes multiplying by −4.
optionRationales.−1/4: The inverse undoes multiplying by −4, so its slope is the reciprocal, 1/(−4) = −1/4.
optionRationales.1/4: This takes the reciprocal but drops the negative; f falls, so its inverse falls too.
optionRationales.−4: −4 is the slope of f; the inverse undoes multiplying by −4.

questions.prompt: Use the inverse workspace to undo f(x)=2x+3 and observe how the graphs of f and f⁻¹ reflect across y=x.

optionRationales.(12−x)/9: Swap x and y in y = 12 − 9x, then solve for y: 9y = 12 − x.
optionRationales.(x−12)/9: This divides by 9 instead of −9, so the sign is lost; the inverse of a falling line also falls.
optionRationales.12−x/9: This divides only x by 9, not the whole 12 − x.
optionRationales.9x−12: This is −f(x), the negative of f, not its inverse.

optionRationales.f⁻¹(3)=1: An inverse sends each output back to its input: 3 came from 1.
optionRationales.f⁻¹(1)=3: This keeps the input and output in the same places; the inverse swaps them.
optionRationales.f⁻¹(3)=−1: An inverse swaps input and output; it does not change their signs.

responses.label: Sales needed for total earnings of $3450

optionRationales.{(8, 4), (6, −6), (3, 3), (−8, 0)}: Each pair has its x and y swapped: (4, 8) becomes (8, 4).
optionRationales.{(4, 8), (−6, 6), (3, 3), (0, −8)}: This is the relation as given; its inverse has to change each pair.
optionRationales.{(−8, −4), (−6, 6), (−3, −3), (8, 0)}: This swaps the coordinates but also changes their signs; finding an inverse never changes signs.

responses.label: Is this inverse relation a function?

optionRationales.yes: Its inputs 8, 6, 3 and −8 are all different, so each input has exactly one output.
optionRationales.no: A relation fails to be a function only when an input repeats with a new output; no x-value repeats here.

optionRationales.(x−10)/5: Swap x and y in y = 5x + 10, then undo the steps: subtract 10, then divide by 5.
optionRationales.5x−10: This changes the sign of +10 but keeps multiplying by 5; an inverse also undoes the multiplication.
optionRationales.(x+10)/5: This undoes the 5 but not the +10: adding 10 again repeats a step of f.
optionRationales.x/5+10: This divides by 5 but keeps the +10; an inverse undoes the +10 first.

optionRationales.5: 5 is the slope of f; the inverse undoes multiplying by 5.
optionRationales.1/5: The inverse undoes multiplying by 5, so its slope is the reciprocal, 1/5.
optionRationales.−1/5: This is the slope of a perpendicular line; an inverse keeps the sign of the slope.
optionRationales.−5: This changes the sign of the slope of f; the inverse undoes multiplying by 5 instead.

optionRationales.−(x+6)/2: Swap x and y in y = −2x − 6, add 6, then divide by −2.
optionRationales.(x+6)/2: This divides by 2 instead of −2, so the sign is lost; the inverse of a falling line also falls.
optionRationales.−2x+6: This changes the sign of −6 but keeps multiplying by −2; an inverse also undoes the multiplication.
optionRationales.(x−6)/2: This subtracts 6 again, repeating a step of f, and divides by 2 instead of −2.

optionRationales.f⁻¹(−12)=3: An inverse sends each output back to its input: −12 came from 3.
optionRationales.f⁻¹(3)=−12: This keeps the input and output in the same places; the inverse swaps them.
optionRationales.f⁻¹(12)=−3: An inverse swaps input and output; it does not change their signs.

questions.prompt: A linear function and its inverse intersect at a point on y=x. If the point is (5,5), what must both functions do there?

optionRationales.0: A point on a graph gives the output at that input; an output of 0 would put the point on the x-axis.
optionRationales.5: (5, 5) is on the graph of f, so f sends 5 to 5.
optionRationales.−5: An output of −5 would make the point (5, −5), which is not on y = x.

optionRationales.0: An inverse swaps the coordinates of each point; swapping (5, 5) cannot produce a 0.
optionRationales.5: Swapping the coordinates of (5, 5) gives (5, 5) again, so the inverse also sends 5 to 5.
optionRationales.−5: An inverse swaps input and output; it does not change their signs.

optionRationales.{(5, −2), (7, 1), (0, 4)}: Each pair has its x and y swapped: (−2, 5) becomes (5, −2).
optionRationales.{(−5, 2), (−7, −1), (0, −4)}: This swaps the coordinates but also changes their signs; finding an inverse never changes signs.
optionRationales.{(−2, 5), (1, 7), (4, 0)}: This is the relation as given; its inverse has to change each pair.

optionRationales.swapping x and y: An inverse undoes the relation, so each output becomes an input: (x, y) turns into (y, x).
optionRationales.negating x and y: Negating both coordinates reflects each point through the origin; it does not undo the relation.
optionRationales.adding x and y: Adding the coordinates gives one number, not a new ordered pair.

optionRationales.(x+9)/4: Swap x and y in y = 4x − 9, then undo the steps: add 9, then divide by 4.
optionRationales.(x−9)/4: This undoes the 4 but not the −9: subtracting 9 again repeats a step of f.
optionRationales.4x+9: This changes the sign of −9 but keeps multiplying by 4; an inverse also undoes the multiplication.
optionRationales.9−4x: This is −f(x), the negative of f, not its inverse.

optionRationales.f⁻¹(15)=6: An inverse sends each output back to its input: 15 came from 6.
optionRationales.f⁻¹(6)=15: This keeps the input and output in the same places; the inverse swaps them.
optionRationales.f⁻¹(15)=−6: An inverse swaps input and output; it does not change their signs.
